newsitem.title: UK: International LPG stable, market in summer doldrum.
newsitem.headline: International LPG stable, market in summer doldrum.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) levels were little moved this week in Europe or Asia as the new round of posted prices failed to lift markets out of their summer doldrums.

Saudi Aramco published its Contract Price (CP), the benchmark against which most Asian LPG is traded, in the middle of the week. Propane fell $3 a tonne from July to $175 a tonne, while butane was unchanged at $192 a tonne.
But the modest propane cut was not enough to excite spot markets in East Asia, a Japanese trader said.
"The market's still losing direction," he said. "The price is almost the same as in July."

Market fundamentals have not altered in Japan, he added, and traders there and in South Korea and China are still waiting for the moment when prices have reached their lowest point of the year before stocking up ahead of the winter.
But with the CP all but unchanged, traders are not sure whether prices have now bottomed out or whether they could go still lower in September.
"The key factor may be the September T1 tender," he said, referring to the first of three monthly spot tenders awarded by Aramco which play a part in the secretive process of setting the CP.

"If the price level falls, then people will think the September CP may be lower," he added. But he said buyers are unlikely to have requirements before the T1 tender, and spot prices are not expected to move significantly before then.

Propane is now talked at around CP -$9/-$6 a tonne fob Mideast Gulf, with butane at around CP -$6/-$4 a tonne, with prices at around CP + $15/$20 a tonne cif Japan for a mixed cargo. Then T1 tender is expected to close on August 8, with bids valid until August 12.

The market is traditionally quiet during the main summer holiday period, and a dealer pointed out that trade in all the major Asian centres is slow. "It's very hot so they don't want to work very hard at the moment," he said.

European activity was hardly more vigorous. A single large propane deal was reported at around $189 a tonne or $190 a tonne cif ARA on Thursday. Bids were heard coming from the low $180s a tonne for most of the week against offers at $190 a tonne. But the only trade seen was done right at the top of that range, indicating that there was some tightness in the market, a trader said.
And butane was discussed thinly in the low to mid $170s a tonne cif NWE, a trader said, although that market was also subdued.
In thin trading conditions, Algerian product was not seen heading to northwest Europe even though the price in the north was high enough to justify it, a trader said.
"There's no Algerian seen, surprisingly," he said. "Economically it could work, but they prefer to send it to the US."
He said that the new August prices issued by Algerian state oil and gas company Sonatrach and by BP had not had any significant impact on market perceptions in Europe.
